title: GOD IS NOT MOCKED: The Terrifying Verse We Quote at Sinners but Forget to Read to Ourselves
paragraphs:
GOD IS NOT MOCKED: The Terrifying Verse We Quote at Sinners but Forget to Read to Ourselves
And strangely, that terrifying truth may be the doorway to the grace you desperately need.
There are some verses we love putting on other people.
“God is not mocked.”
We say it when somebody openly rebels against God.
We post it when culture celebrates something Scripture condemns.
We remember it when an arrogant person seems to be getting away with evil.
And yes, the warning is real.
But there is something uncomfortable about Galatians 6:7 that we sometimes miss.
Paul was not standing in a pagan marketplace shouting this sentence at unbelievers.
He was writing to people inside the church.
People who knew the language of faith.
People who had heard the Gospel.
People who could say the right things about God.
People disturbingly similar to us.
And before you keep reading, understand where this is going.
This is not an article about “those terrible people out there.”
This is about the seed in your hand.
The seed in mine.
The secret decisions nobody applauds and nobody sees.
The compromises we keep watering.
The repentance we keep postponing.
The habits we excuse because judgment has not arrived yet.
The private things we assume will somehow never become a harvest.
Paul writes:
—Galatians 6:7
The Greek makes the warning even more piercing:
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.”
Mē planasthe, Theos ou myktērizetai; ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
“Do not be deceived. God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
Notice how Paul begins.
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.”
Mē planasthe.
Do not be deceived.
Before Paul speaks about mocking God, he speaks about deception.
Because one of sin’s greatest powers is not merely making evil attractive.
It makes consequences look impossible.
Sin whispers:
Nothing happened last time.
Nobody knows.
You can stop whenever you want.
God understands.
It isn't really hurting anyone.
You still pray.
You still go to church.
You still post Bible verses.
You still believe in Jesus.
So surely everything is fine.
That is the deception.
Then Paul says:
“Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται.”
Theos ou myktērizetai.
God is not mocked.
The verb translated “mocked” is μυκτηρίζω (myktērizō). It carries the sense of treating someone with contempt or derision—of sneering at someone as though they can be dismissed.
Paul's point is far deeper than “Don't make jokes about God.”
This is about attempting to treat the living God as though His moral order can be ignored.
As though we can plant one thing and demand that He give us another.
Plant lust and demand purity.
Plant bitterness and demand peace.
Plant dishonesty and demand trust.
Plant pride and demand spiritual intimacy.
Plant neglect and demand a flourishing marriage.
Plant cruelty and demand healthy relationships.
Plant secret sin and demand public anointing.
Plant spiritual laziness and wonder why our souls feel empty.
Plant years into the flesh and then become angry with God when the harvest does not resemble heaven.
That is the insanity Paul exposes.
We want to choose the seed and command God to change the harvest.
But God is not mocked.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about sowing is that harvests do not normally appear immediately.
You can sow today and still smile tonight.
You can compromise today and still sing worship songs on Sunday.
You can betray someone's trust and still receive compliments.
You can feed an addiction and still function at work.
You can carry bitterness for years and still call yourself forgiving.
You can maintain a hidden life while everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
That delay can become its own form of deception.
Because when consequences are delayed, we begin confusing God's patience with God's approval.
But Scripture warns us against precisely that mistake.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we presume upon the riches of God's kindness, patience, and forbearance, failing to recognize that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Read that carefully.
His patience is not permission.
His kindness is an invitation.
His delay is mercy.
The fact that God has not exposed you does not mean He endorses what you are hiding.
The fact that you woke up this morning is not evidence that sin does not matter.
It may be evidence that mercy has given you another morning to repent.
And that changes everything.
Because “God is not mocked” is not merely a threat hanging over a sinner.
In Christ, it can become an alarm clock.
Wake up.
Come home.
Stop pretending.
Put down the shovel.
Stop planting what is destroying you.
There is still time to surrender the field.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your children do not know.
Your friends see your smile but not what happens when the room gets quiet.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe your bank statement exposes priorities your mouth would never admit.
Maybe there is a conversation you keep deleting.
A resentment you keep feeding.
An affair of the heart you keep calling harmless.
A secret addiction.
An obsession.
A lie you have repeated so many times that you almost believe it.
A person you refuse to forgive.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A private compromise you have renamed so you no longer have to call it sin.
And somewhere inside, you keep thinking:
I will deal with it later.
That sentence has buried more spiritual lives than we realize.
Later.
Later I will repent.
Later I will forgive.
Later I will confess.
Later I will return to Scripture.
Later I will become serious about Jesus.
Later I will repair what I damaged.
Later I will stop.
But every “later” plants another seed.
Paul continues:
“For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.”
—Galatians 6:8
This is the context we cannot remove from “God is not mocked.”
Paul is describing two directions of life.
The flesh.
The Spirit.
And the question becomes painfully personal:
What are you feeding?
Not what do you claim to believe.
Not what Christian label do you use.
Not what verse is written in your bio.
What are you actually feeding?
Because eventually, what we repeatedly feed begins feeding on us.
That secret anger changes the way you speak.
That pornography changes the way you see people.
That envy makes another person's blessing feel like your punishment.
That greed teaches you that “enough” is always one purchase away.
That pride makes correction feel like persecution.
That unforgiveness allows someone who wounded you years ago to continue occupying your heart today.
That constant hunger for human approval slowly makes obedience to God feel dangerous.
Seeds become habits.
Habits become patterns.
Patterns shape character.
And character has consequences.
This is why biblical grace must never be reduced to God shrugging at sin.
Grace is far more beautiful than that.
Grace does not merely tell guilty people, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross tells us sin mattered so profoundly that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus did not die because rebellion was insignificant.
He died because we could not save ourselves from it.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
—1 Peter 2:24
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Justice and mercy met at the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ endured the cross.
Christ rose from the dead.
And now forgiveness is offered not because we have successfully cleaned ourselves up, but because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
That is where this warning becomes breathtaking.
The God who cannot be mocked is also the God who receives repentant sinners.
The God who sees everything is the God from whom you no longer need to hide.
The God who knows the scandal is the God who offers grace.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then fear entered the room.
One accusation.
Another.
Then another.
And the man who said he would die with Jesus denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing your own voice say the words you swore you would never say.
Imagine realizing that Jesus had already told you this would happen.
Peter's failure was real.
His tears were real.
His scandal was real.
But his scandal was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because grace can restore what sin has shattered.
Peter's story did not end beside a charcoal fire of denial.
Jesus met him again beside another charcoal fire in John 21.
Failure met mercy.
Shame met restoration.
The fallen disciple heard Christ call him forward again.
“Follow me.”
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not rewriting evil as good.
Not calling darkness light.
Jesus does something infinitely greater.
He redeems sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you need that sentence more than you expected.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But grace is not permission to keep writing the same rebellion forever.
Jesus does not merely offer you a prettier version of your old life.
He calls you to Himself.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not earning forgiveness.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because the Holy Spirit has opened your eyes to see that the thing you were embracing is killing you and Christ is better.
This is why the Gospel destroys both despair and presumption.
Despair says:
“I have gone too far. Jesus could never forgive someone like me.”
The cross answers:
Christ saves sinners.
Presumption says:
“I can continue deliberately embracing sin because Jesus will forgive me anyway.”
The cross answers:
You were purchased at an immeasurable price. Do not treat grace as permission to cherish the very rebellion from which Christ came to redeem you.
Grace neither tells the broken sinner to stay away nor tells the comfortable sinner to stay asleep.
Grace says:
Come to Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come exposed.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
But come ready to surrender.
Perhaps that is why this verse feels so sharp.
“God is not mocked.”
There is nowhere to hide.
And maybe that is good news.
Because hiding is exhausting.
Maintaining two versions of yourself is exhausting.
Pretending you are okay is exhausting.
Managing appearances while your soul is bleeding is exhausting.
Explaining away conviction is exhausting.
Running from God is exhausting.
Adam discovered that in Eden.
After sin came hiding.
But God called:
“Where are you?”
Not because an omniscient God had misplaced Adam.
The question brought the hiding man into the open.
And perhaps, through these words, God is asking something similar of you.
Where are you?
Not your Facebook version.
Not your church version.
Not the version everybody congratulates.
You.
Where are you?
What have you been sowing?
What are you becoming?
What are you hiding?
What are you refusing to surrender?
What would happen if Jesus touched the one room in your life you keep locked?
This is the moment when some people close the article.
Don't.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
For those who belong to Christ, conviction is not God gleefully crushing you.
The Holy Spirit exposes darkness to lead us toward truth, repentance, restoration, and deeper fellowship with Christ.
The enemy wants exposure to end in hopelessness.
Jesus brings sinners into the light so healing and transformation can begin.
So stop negotiating with the seed.
Stop asking how close you can live to sin without consequences.
Ask a better question:
How completely can I belong to Jesus?
And if you have failed again?
Run toward Christ.
If you have fallen?
Run toward Christ.
If yesterday was ugly?
Run toward Christ.
If your secret finally came into the light?
Run toward Christ.
If consequences remain even after forgiveness?
Walk through them with Christ.
If repentance requires an apology, make it.
If integrity requires confession, seek wise and biblically appropriate help and tell the truth.
If temptation requires boundaries, build them.
If a relationship continually leads you into rebellion, stop pretending proximity to sin is strength.
If you need mature Christian accountability, seek it.
If something keeps feeding your flesh, stop feeding it.
Then begin sowing differently.
Open Scripture when you would normally scroll.
Pray when anxiety tells you to panic.
Forgive when your flesh demands revenge.
Give when greed says hoard.
Tell the truth when lying would be easier.
Turn your eyes away when lust tells you to stare.
Serve when pride demands attention.
Worship when despair says God has abandoned you.
Return when shame tells you to disappear.
These things do not purchase salvation.
Jesus purchased redemption.
We obey because grace has changed the direction of our lives.
And don't miss what comes immediately after Paul's warning.
Galatians 6:9 says:
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.”
There is another harvest.
Maybe you needed to hear that too.
Not every seed you planted was evil.
Some of you have been praying for years.
Keep sowing.
Some of you have been resisting a temptation nobody knows exists.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are raising children and wondering whether anything you teach them is reaching their hearts.
Keep sowing.
Some of you chose forgiveness even though the wound still hurts.
Keep sowing.
Some of you returned to Jesus after years away and are frustrated because transformation feels slower than you expected.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are serving while nobody notices.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are fighting to rebuild a marriage, restore integrity, renew your mind, break destructive patterns, and learn obedience one difficult day at a time.
Do not grow weary.
The God who is not mocked is also the God who sees faithfulness nobody else sees.
And that makes Galatians 6:7 more than frightening.
It makes it hopeful.
Seeds matter.
Your choices matter.
Faithfulness matters.
Repentance matters.
What you do when nobody watches matters.
And above all, Jesus matters.
Maybe this article found you while you are standing between two fields.
One contains what you have been sowing.
The other contains what, by God's grace, you could begin sowing today.
You cannot return to yesterday and remove every seed.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
Some apologies may still need to be made.
Some trust may require time to rebuild.
Some wounds need patient healing.
But you can bring your life to Jesus Christ.
And He is still in the business of redeeming people whose stories looked ruined.
That is why Gospel Warrior will never preach behavior modification without Christ.
We do not need motivational Christianity.
We need Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness.
Breaking chains.
Restoring the fallen.
Transforming hearts.
Making old things new.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already begun restoring a chapter you thought was beyond redemption, tell your testimony. Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be final.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Not somebody you want to “teach a lesson.”
Someone you love.
Someone drifting.
Someone hiding.
Someone exhausted from maintaining appearances.
Someone who believes his or her scandal is too ugly for grace.
Your share might put the truth in front of them at the exact moment they were preparing to give up.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because some truths need to confront us more than once.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand biblical truth, heal through the Gospel, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, stay close.
Supporting a ministry is not what saves you.
We are saved by God's grace through faith, not by purchasing access to religious content.

But Scripture does teach willing generosity and partnership in Gospel work. If God has blessed you with the ability and you genuinely believe this ministry is bearing biblical fruit, supporting it can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership—freely given, never coerced.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Give freely where God leads you to give.
Serve.
Pray.
Love people.
Support faithful Gospel work according to your ability.
And never turn money into the measure of someone's devotion to Jesus.
Christ already paid the price that matters most.
So tonight, before you close this article, forget everybody else for a moment.
Forget the person you thought needed to read this.
Look at your own field.
What have you been planting?
What seed is in your hand right now?
Because tomorrow's harvest is being touched by today's surrender.
God is not mocked.
But neither is His grace exhausted by the repentant sinner who comes home through Jesus Christ.
The God who sees the seed also sees the tears.
The God who sees the scandal also sees what Christ can redeem.
And perhaps the chapter you are most ashamed of is not where your story ends.
The seed may explain your yesterday—but surrendered to Jesus, your yesterday does not have to own your tomorrow.
